pulls.title: test: check ParseByteUnits overflow boundary
pulls.body:
I added this small test for `ParseByteUnits` because I noticed the overflow check in `src/util/strencodings.cpp` is only tested with `18446744073709551615g`. If you change `>` to `>=`, no existing test fails, and the fuzz target only checks that it doesn't crash, not the return value.

This adds the boundary cases for `K` (1024): `18014398509481983K` (the max value that fits in `uint64_t`, returning `18'446'744'073'709'550'592`) and `18014398509481984K` (the first value that overflows). With this, changing `>` to `>=` makes `util_tests/util_ParseByteUnits` fail.

pulls.title: wallet: Handle or explicitly ignore `WalletBatch` write failures
pulls.body:
A common theme in the wallet is that many database write failures are ignored, when they should probably be handled, or at least documented that a failure is being ignored. This PR marks all database functions in `WalletBatch` as `[[nodiscard]]` so that a compiler will tell us if a return value is implicitly ignored. All of the calls to those functions are updated to either deal with failure, or explicitly ignore it with a rationale.

Based on #35752 which handles failures for the encryption functions.

pulls.title: validation: prefetch blocks while connecting
pulls.body:
**Problem:** Connecting a block already on disk requires reading and deserializing it.
Doing this on the validation thread stalls validation and slows reindexing and initial block download.

This is a follow-up to [#35295](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/35295), which parallelized input prevout fetching during block connection.

**Fix:** Add a `Chainstate`-owned block fetcher that reads later blocks from disk while the current block is connected.
Start with synchronous 1-block read-ahead, then move reads to an eagerly started worker pool that persists across activations.
Keep caller-provided blocks on the direct path and refill a sliding read-ahead window.
During reorgs, start reading the first sibling while disconnecting the old tip.
Retry speculative failures synchronously when the block is needed.

`-blockfetchthreads=<n>` selects readers per chainstate, with a default of 2 and a cap of 16.
Setting it to 0 disables read-ahead. The window retains up to two blocks per reader, giving 4 by default.
Measurements favor 2 readers with a window of 4 or 8 blocks, so the default uses the smaller window.

**Credit:** The idea comes from [bitcoindev1337](https://bitcoin-irc.chaincode.com/bitcoin-core-dev/2026-08-11#1245429), who had already implemented a similar design and reported comparable results.

pulls.title: rpc, descriptor: warn when multipath expansion clones single-path key expressions
pulls.body:
This PR:
  - deduplicate warnings pushed with `PushWarnings` in RPC calls
  - warn when single-path key expressions or tr() subscripts are cloned into every multipath expansion; surfaced by `importdescriptors` and by a new `warnings` field on `getdescriptorinfo` (which also exposes the existing miniscript `older()` warnings)

Cloning internal to musig() is not warned: both `musig(A,B)/<0;1>/*` and `musig(A/<1;2>,B)` derive a distinct aggregate key per branch, so nothing observable is reused.

closes #35985

pulls.title: orphanage: Fix orphan reconsideration disconnect hole, add 1p1c invariant harness
pulls.body:
The first commit adds `p2p_1p1c_liveness`, an end-to-end fuzz target for parent and child relay. It
  drives a real PeerManager with real messages and validation, and checks that if an honest peer announces
  the child of an acceptable parent and child, the child reaches the mempool within a bounded time,
  whatever other peers do. Known liveness holes are marked in the target as flags that turn the check off
  once opened, including this one. With that flag turned off, the target finds this bug on master from an
  empty corpus in under an hour on one core; an earlier version found it first
  (https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/36371#issuecomment-5937814761).

  The second commit hands reconsideration over to a remaining announcer when the marked announcement is
  erased, and removes the flag.

Follow-up PR to fill the holes is here: https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/36506

pulls.title: txorphanage: bound orphan memory by storing transactions serialized
pulls.body:
The orphanage limits the "usage" of the orphans it stores, per peer and globally, to bound the amount of memory an attacker can make us hold on to. It uses weight as a proxy for that memory, on the assumption that weight is "often higher than the actual memory usage of the transaction".

That assumption does not hold for a deserialized transaction. Every witness stack element is an individually heap-allocated vector, costing its 24-byte slot in the stack vector plus a 32-byte minimum allocation, while only weighing 2WU. A transaction of 199,000 1-byte witness elements weighs 398,247WU (i.e. it is of standard weight, and witness standardness cannot be checked while the inputs are missing), but uses 11.1MB of memory: 28 times what is accounted for it, and one such orphan can be retained per peer.

Rather than change the accounting metric, keep orphans in serialized form, deserializing them again on the paths that hand them back out. Serialized, a transaction's memory usage is bounded by its weight, so the existing weight-based accounting becomes a true upper bound on memory and the worst case is the peers' combined allowances.

Admission, eviction and accounting behavior are unchanged: no transaction that was previously accepted is refused, so orphan resolution (and thus 1p1c package relay) keeps working for standard-weight transactions whose witnesses consist of many small elements, such as BitVM-style transactions.

pulls.title: index: batch db writes during initial sync
pulls.body:
Pending on #34897 review. Please go there first.

---------------------------------

Decouples part of #26966.

Right now, index initial sync writes to disk for every block, which is not the best for HDD. This change batches those, so disk writes are less frequent during initial sync. This also cuts down `cs_main` contention by reducing the number of `NextBlockSync` calls (instead of calling it for every block, we will call it once per block window), making the node more responsive (IBD and validation) while indexes sync up. On top of that, it lays the groundwork for the bigger speedups, since part of the parallelization pre-work is already in place.

Just as a small summary:

* Batch DB writes instead of flushing per block, which improves sync time on HDD due to the reduced number of disk write operations.
* Reduce `cs_main` lock contention, which improves the overall node responsiveness (and primarily IBD) while the indexes threads are syncing.
* Lays the groundwork for the real speedups, since part of #26966 parallelization pre-work is introduced here as well.
* Reduces the number of generated LDB files. See l0rinc's [comment](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/34489#issuecomment-3876972773).

pulls.title: [wip,nomerge,rfc] build: Require C++23 compiler
pulls.body:
C++23 for Bitcoin Core is mostly a "style update" on top of C++20. However, the workarounds to avoid C++23 keep accumulating and some parts of the code already use C++23 features, such as lambda attributes (https://github.com/bitcoin-core/libmultiprocess/commit/bdd0cd69418d189f62699d274a751cbf6d36bb43).

I don't know when it is fine to switch, but at some point, I think it is fine to require a C++23 compiler, so that [new stuff](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/34979#issuecomment-4448399166) is unlocked. Of course this requires bumping the minimum required compiler versions:

* GCC: 13
* Clang: 19

There are some C++23 features that aren't implemented (such as `<stacktrace>` not really shipped in any vanilla stdlib today), or e.g. `ranges::starts_with` not implemented until libstdc++-16. But overall I think we are better off using C++23 without those few features instead of waiting longer?

pulls.title: mining: use a steady clock for the getblocktemplate rebuild interval
pulls.body:
Based on #36356 and #36921. **Only the last commit is new.**

After a mempool change, `getblocktemplate` only rebuilds its cached template once it's more than 5 seconds old, and it measures that age with the system clock. That works fine in practice, but as pointed out in a [review comment](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/36356#discussion_r4562199844), a steady clock is the better fit for measuring an interval, since system time changes don't affect it.

This switches to the steady clock, like #30372 did for `RandAddSeedPerfmon`. Since `setmocktime` doesn't move it, `mining_prioritisetransaction.py` now waits out the 5 seconds, and the unit test uses a fake steady clock.

pulls.title: test: fix coinbases built on arbitrary parents
pulls.body:
**Problem:** Test helpers that attach active-tip templates to arbitrary parents retain the template's subsidy.
Existing reorg tests can pass with underpaid coinbases.
A fork crossing a halving can overpay and fail with `bad-cb-amount`.
At heights 1 through 16, encoding only the height leaves the coinbase input script too short and triggers `bad-cb-length`.

**Fix:** Share parent-dependent reconstruction between `BuildChain()` and `MinerTestingSetup::Block()`, deriving difficulty and coinbase fields from the actual parent.
Pad rebuilt coinbase input scripts.
Require coinbase-only templates so replacing the reward with the subsidy cannot discard transaction fees.

pulls.title: wallet: make migration more robust against failures
pulls.body:
This is just me finding a few more edge cases after #34156 and #34176

The goal of the PR is to handle failures in a controlled way. Just so the process can automatically restore the original wallet without requiring user manual intervention.

The covered cases are:

1. During `DoMigration()`: There are methods that can throw exceptions and abruptly abort the process. 
Instead of crashing (GUI) or returning a generic exception, we now will catch and return the error gracefully. This lets the process restore the original wallet automatically.

2. Trying to migrate a wallet in a read-only directory throws a filesystem exception and skips cleanup.
 Now the process will fail gracefully with a clear error msg, and automatically restore the original wallet.

3. Any failure during `MigrateToSQLite` requires user manual intervention. 
Now the original wallet db will remain untouched, and only be updated once the sqlite db creation fully succeeds.

pulls.title: wallet: harden external signer psbt processing, revamp mock
pulls.body:
The current external signer functional test mock can only echo a prepared PSBT. This gets in the way of testing more complicated scenarios, i.e. misbehaving signers and (MuSig2) multisig.

- *test: have external signer mock use a wallet*: gives the mock its own offline node and wallet with private keys, while the test uses the watch-only version.
- *external_signer: require matching PSBT versions*
- *external_signer: merge PSBT response instead of replacing*: tests signers that drop outputs, reduce their value or change the script. Merging rejects these changes while allowing signers to omit unnecessary PSBT fields.
- *external_signer: reject unsafe sighash types*
- *external_signer: **reject finalized PSBT inputs***: keeps the above check simple. Documents this new requirement. HWI does not finalize.

The remaining commits prepare the test helpers and enforce IWYU for `src/external_signer.cpp`.

This PR absorbs the scenarios from #35358, but is better able to test them thanks to the new mock signer implementation.

This PR does not intend to fully harden against a malicious external signer, and can't protect against a malicious HWI (equivalent) process running as the same user.

pulls.title: [Demo] validation: remove AssumeUTXO
pulls.body:
**Draft demo:** this is meant to showcase what complete AssumeUTXO removal could look like and the simplifications that AssumeUTXO currently prevents.
The decision about complete removal is of course still open. This draft is meant to serve as a concrete reference for the smaller proposals below - it's not meant to be merged.

**Smaller PRs:** I will carve out individual changes to gauge interest in each part, and link them here as they are opened.
Some of the findings are useful even if snapshot loading or background validation stays.
Feedback on which parts seem worth pursuing, and in which order, is welcome.

**Motivation:** this follows our in-person discussion at the October 2026 Core Dev meeting.
My impression was that there was rough agreement about the ambiguity background validation introduces: we trust a snapshot enough to use it immediately, but describe that trust as temporary until the same node finishes checking history.

Multiple chainstates affect much more than snapshot loading: ordinary validation changes have to account for different chainstate roles, candidate sets, notifications, downloads, pruning, cache allocation, database lifetimes and locks.
I am not sure this amount of complexity in the most critical part of our codebase is still worth it, given that adoption [isn't where we hoped it would be](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/35054#issuecomment-4468360424).
Ordinary IBD is also getting faster: #35295 is already merged, and the upcoming `pruneassumevalid` will make pruned IBD even faster.

Snapshot bootstrapping without background validation can still offer an advantage: a new node becomes usable before ordinary IBD would finish because snapshot loading time scales with the UTXO set size, while ordinary IBD time scales with the blockchain size.
Whether that is worth its maintenance cost is a fair question, and we can discuss it here or in the dedicated PR where I will propose the removal.
Even after removal, we could decide to add it back in a cleaner way, for example isolated through IPC.
This demo makes that cost, and the code we could remove, visible for that discussion.

**Background validation can be considered separately:** if we keep snapshot loading, I would prefer making its trust assumption explicit and distributing verification across ordinary IBD nodes, as proposed in #32377 and #36543.
That could give us wider independent checking of the commitment without making every snapshot user maintain a second chainstate.

Users who want to validate history themselves and transition to an archival node could rebuild with `-reindex` and pruning disabled.
Alternatively, they could run IBD in a separate datadir while their snapshot node remains usable, then switch once it is ready.
@Sjors's #36557 discusses dropping mandatory background sync and these alternatives.

**What the series demonstrates:**

* After the fixture cleanup in #36601, the next eight commits remove background validation while snapshot loading keeps working, a stopping point that can be reviewed on its own.
* The middle commits remove snapshot imports and startup resumption, then the validation, block storage, notification and release-process special cases they needed.
* The final seven commits add the simplifications this removal enables: startup in one pass, stable database ownership, one download path, a single prune height, and removal of the locks and diagnostics used to select and identify chainstates.

Ordinary validation, `-assumevalid`, pruning, `ChainstateManager` and UTXO export (`dumptxoutset`) remain.

**Related work:**

* [AJ's recent faster-loader branch](https://github.com/ajtowns/bitcoin/tree/202610-loadtxoutset-speedy) and [Sjors's chunked-import experiments](https://github.com/Sjors/bitcoin/tree/2026/10/utxo-coin-chunks) explore reducing import overhead while retaining snapshot support.
* #35054 contains the broader discussion about P2P snapshot distribution, its users and its costs.

pulls.title: validation: avoid partial override of non-valid validation state
pulls.body:
ValidationState::Error() only sets the reject reason if the state is still valid. When it is called on a state that is already Invalid or Error, the mode changes but the earlier reason, result and debug message are kept. The result is a mix of the old and new error. Code review in #35570 found two places where this happens. This makes the in-and-out use of the state parameter harder to follow and to remove later.

This PR makes both cases explicit:

1. `ConnectBlock()` → `CheckBlock()` with a mutated block (`BLOCK_MUTATED`, e.g. a merkle root mismatch). This is treated as a sign of corruption and reported through `FatalError()`, but the resulting Error state kept `BLOCK_MUTATED` / `bad-txnmrklroot`. Now the Invalid state is logged and then replaced, so the Error state carries the corruption message.

2. `ActivateBestChainStep()` → `DisconnectTip()` → `FlushStateToDisk()` failure. `FlushStateToDisk()` has already reported a fatal error, and `ActivateBestChainStep()` then called `FatalError()` a second time with a less specific message. Now the existing error is logged and returned unchanged, and no second fatal error is reported.

Behavior changes:

- Case 1: the returned state has the reject reason "Corrupt block found indicating potential hardware failure.", no result and no debug message. The original reason is logged.
- Case 2: the duplicate fatal-error notification is no longer sent. The returned reject reason does not change.

The first commit adds a unit test for case 1 that captures the current behavior, and the second commit updates its expectations. Case 2 has no test, because a flush failure cannot be triggered without fault injection. The path where `DisconnectTip()` fails while the state is still valid is covered by `feature_abortnode.py` and is unchanged.

pulls.title: Keep witness stacks in serialized form in CScriptWitness
pulls.body:
This is split off from #36521. This PR focuses on reducing memory usage of transactions in memory, leaving performance improvements for other PRs.

`CScriptWitness` stores a witness stack as a `std::vector<std::vector<unsigned char>>`, which costs a 24-byte vector object and an allocation for every non-empty element. This makes it possible to construct transactions that take a large amount of memory after deserialization.

This PR first introduces encapsulation for `CScriptWitness`, hiding its representation. The last commit then changes the representation to be single `std::unique_ptr<byte[]>` which for non-empty witness stacks stores their serialization prefixed by a small length header. Witnesses can no longer be modified in place; they can only be replaced in their entirety. Access to the individual witness stack elements is done by on-the-fly deserialization instead.

`CScriptWitness` shrinks from 24 to 8 bytes, and `CTxIn` from 112 to 96 bytes. Worst-case allocated size for transactions kept in memory drops from roughly 28 bytes/WU to 1.6 bytes/WU.

This worsens deserialization and validation time, adding some 50-70 ms per block to the worst case for me. A follow-up #36918 with optimizations improves the worst case deserialization time significantly instead. Other minor degradations:
* libbitcoinkernel's witness stack element accessor becomes $\mathcal{O}(n)$ in the index of the witness element; using it to iterate a whole witness may therefore become $\mathcal{O}(n^2)$.
* `CScriptWitness::back()` is $\mathcal{O}(n)$ in the length of the witness stack.

Issue reported by furszy and 0xB10C.

pulls.title: wallet, migration: Contain all legacy wallet and migration related things in its own subdirectory, namespace, and classes
pulls.body:
Originally, legacy wallet migration was built upon the foundation of being able to load legacy wallets. Now that we no longer support loading legacy wallets, there is no reason to keep any of the legacy wallet loading and migration code in the main wallet objects. Having this co-mingling of never-to-be-changed legacy wallet code and new descriptor wallet code makes it difficult to implement new things into the wallet.

This PR fully separates out all of the legacy wallet related things into a subdirectory `wallet/legacy`, with everything in that directory under a `wallet::legacy_migration` namespace so as to prevent accidental usage outside of legacy wallets. This includes a little bit of duplication with current loading code, but not that much, and we are able to both remove unrelated descriptor wallet loading from the legacy wallet loading, and unrelated legacy wallet loading from normal descriptor wallet loading.

`LegacyWallet` is introduced as a subclass of `CWallet` which contains all of the relevant legacy wallet and migration functions so that `CWallet` cannot accidentally use some legacy wallet function. Additionally, `LegacyDataSPKM` is moved into a new file and this new namespace so that it cannot be used outside of migration.

Lastly, `ReorderTransactions` is a legacy wallet only function that is also moved into `LegacyWallet`.

Builds upon #34909, and depends on #36823 for removing some functions that were previously used by migration.

pulls.title: kernel: add btck_witness_stack_get_items
pulls.body:
With the change on #36895 : 
> libbitcoinkernel's witness stack element accessor becomes O(n) in the index of the witness element; using it to iterate a whole witness may therefore become O(n^2).

This adds `btck_witness_stack_get_items` which reads the stack in one O(n) pass and writes each item's pointer and size into two arrays passed to it. `WitnessStackApi::GetItems` is the C++ wrapper. The pointers are valid as long as the witness stack exists.

An earlier version passed each item to a callback from the bottom of the stack to the top. That order followed the serialization, which can only be read from the bottom up, more than how a stack should actually be read. This version lets the items be read from either end.

pulls.title: mining: use steady clock for waitNext timeout
pulls.body:
Follow up suggested in https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/36791#discussion_r4568050151.

`waitNext` measures its timeout and 1-second fee tick with the wall clock, while `waitTipChanged` uses the steady clock. This means a wall clock jump changes how long `waitNext` waits, and it never times out while mocktime is frozen.

Use the steady clock for the deadline and tick. `NodeClock` is kept only for the testnet 20-minute rule, which must compare node time with the tip's timestamp.

pulls.title: ci: add native freeBSD ci job
pulls.body:
This replaces the FreeBSD cross-compilation job with a native build and test job inside a FreeBSD VM. NetBSD and OpenBSD retain their existing cross-compilation jobs.

We currently cross-compile BSD binaries without testing them in this repository. Running tests before merge should help catch platform-specific regressions that would otherwise first appear in nightly builds. This starts with FreeBSD because it has been the most reliable BSD platform in the nightly jobs.

As we don't have native FreeBSD runners, the job uses [vmactions/freebsd-vm](https://github.com/vmactions/freebsd-vm), which is also used by the nightly builds. It reuses the existing CI scripts, depends build, and cache actions where possible.

The VM image is cached after its `prepare` step installs dependencies. The job also restores and saves the usual build caches. Initial testing on free GitHub Actions runners took approximately 60 minutes without caches and 20–30 minutes with caches populated. Performance on Warp runners remains untested.

The VM uses the runner's available CPU count and 75% of its RAM, leaving the remaining memory for the host and VM overhead. There is some overhead after testing while `rsync` copies cache directories back out of the VM.

The patchset also suppresses `lsof` warnings on FreeBSD that would otherwise interfere with functional tests.

The job requires enabling one additional action:

```text
vmactions/freebsd-vm@v1
```

pulls.title: validation: Leave some pruned blocks in `m_blocks_unlinked`, fix another `nSequenceId` issue
pulls.body:
`m_blocks_unlinked` serves two purposes:
 1. finding blocks to `setBlockIndexCandidates` once their parents are
       received
 2. setting `m_chain_tx_count` once the parents are received

In case the parent block of a previously pruned block is received,  2. is currently not being done, because pruning removed the entries from `m_blocks_unlinked`.
This can result in `CheckBlockIndex` failures (#31512, #36021) and incorrect rpc results, plus we are in a temporarily inconsistent state (`m_chain_tx_count` is currently not set, but would get set if we restarted).

This scenario is unlikely to happen during normal node operation unless there are huge reorgs, but it can happen, for example, in `getblockfrompeer` scenarios.
Fix this by leaving pruned blocks in `m_blocks_unlinked` that don't have `m_chain_tx_count` set, and also adding them on restart. 

This was one of two reasons, the fuzz target `block_index_tree` couldn't cover pruning of blocks not in the main chain.

The other one is similar to #34521 and #35070 - if we receive a block a second time (after pruning), we could change `nSequenceId` while the block is in `setBlockIndexCandidates` - fix this by attempting to remove it from the set before re-adding it.

After the two issues are fixed, the restriction from `block_index_tree` fuzz target is removed.

Fixes #36021
Fixes #31512

pulls.title: wallet: fill PSBT_GLOBAL_XPUB
pulls.body:
Closes #27583.

`PSBT_GLOBAL_XPUB` already serializes, deserializes and merges when PSBTs are combined. Nothing writes it, so a PSBT produced by the wallet never carries it, and a signer that only has the file cannot rebuild the multisig from it. Today Specter [fills the field itself](https://github.com/cryptoadvance/specter-desktop/blob/8843e2f0640a9adc129f9ab6afe5ecb9632e7c5b/src/cryptoadvance/specter/wallet/wallet.py#L1866-L1881) after getting the PSBT from Core.

<details><summary>Before and after with the BitBox02 and Trezor simulators</summary>

A 2-of-3 `wsh(sortedmulti(...))` on regtest with the simulator as one co-signer, signed through HWI 3.2.0. The "before" file is the same PSBT with its `PSBT_GLOBAL_XPUB` records removed, so nothing else differs.

| | without the field | with the field |
|---|---|---|
| BitBox02 | refuses, `This BitBox02 is not one of the cosigners` | signs |
| Trezor T | signs, co-signer nodes sent with zeroed chain codes and no derivation paths | signs, nodes sent with the real chain codes and paths |

What `parse_multisig` hands the Trezor for the change output:

```
without: global xpubs=0  zeroed chain codes=3/3  depths=[0, 0, 0]  paths=[[], [], []]
with   : global xpubs=3  zeroed chain codes=0/3  depths=[4, 4, 4]  paths=[[1, 0], [1, 0], [1, 0]]
```

</details>

A new `Descriptor` accessor returns the extended keys a descriptor is built from, and `DescriptorScriptPubKeyMan::FillPSBT` writes those of every descriptor with an input or an output in the PSBT. That covers `walletcreatefundedpsbt`, `walletprocesspsbt`, `send`, `sendall`, `psbtbumpfee` and the GUI send dialog, which all go through `CWallet::FillPSBT`.

Only the keys BIP 174 allows are added, the ones that derive, through unhardened steps alone, a key their descriptor produced, listed in the PSBT at the origin the descriptor gave it. So a key expression ending in `/*h` adds nothing.

Whoever holds a PSBT from the wallet can now derive the addresses of the descriptors it uses. Setting `bip32derivs` to false in `walletcreatefundedpsbt` or `walletprocesspsbt` stops the wallet from adding the field, along with the derivation paths, and does not remove what a PSBT already carries.

`descriptorprocesspsbt` is left out, since it signs from the descriptors it is given without going through the wallet, and I intend to cover it as a follow-up.

pulls.title: mining: include chunks that reach block limits
pulls.body:
**Problem:** `BlockAssembler` fills block templates with mempool chunks that fit the configured weight limit and the consensus sigops limit, but currently rejects a chunk when it brings either total exactly to its limit.
Equality is valid because [`block_max_weight` is a maximum](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/blob/b811aeabad94ef48cd0f0fb1d2fcc456594aeedb/src/node/mining_types.h#L59-L65) and [BIP 141 defines both consensus limits using `≤`](https://github.com/bitcoin/bips/blob/master/bip-0141.mediawiki#other-consensus-critical-limits).
The `>=` checks can therefore leave valid capacity unused and omit a fee-paying chunk.
Mining option validation also permits [`block_max_weight == MAX_BLOCK_WEIGHT`](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/blob/ed7dd7cf4e1561a97edf72eba29a67b14e28c717/src/node/mining_args.cpp#L43-L46) and [`coinbase_output_max_additional_sigops == MAX_BLOCK_SIGOPS_COST`](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/blob/ed7dd7cf4e1561a97edf72eba29a67b14e28c717/src/node/mining_args.cpp#L55-L59), while the chunk checks reject an accounted total equal to either limit.
A [2016 review comment on the original package-selection PR](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/7600#discussion_r67020333) raised the same inclusive-limit point.

**Fix:** Use strict greater-than comparisons so exact-limit chunks are included.
Extend the existing chunk-limit test to cover exact fits and one-unit overages for both weight and sigops.
Clarify how mining software reserves weight and sigops for the completed block.

This addresses the first issue in #35596.

pulls.title: init: Fix surprising behaviors of negated options
pulls.body:
While looking into #36759 I discovered `-notorcontrol` did the opposite of what would be expected from it and I then checked for similar issues in other init options. There are several more where `-nofoo` does something surprising including one of them crashing the node.

This PR attempts to fix all these surprising behaviors while also keeping things as simple as possible and just change behavior to something that makes sense harmless in the context of the option. Fixes that use a common approach for the fix are grouped together into a commit even if the options included themselves may have no relation at all.

| Commit | Problematic options behavior | Fix approach |
|---|---|---|
| [mempool: Reject cluster limits below 1](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/commit/512773d111daaa4330c873ed5889b9ef511f6e3a) | `-nolimitclustercount` hits an assertion in `TxGraph` on the first mempool transaction. `-nolimitclustersize` rejects every transaction. | Reject values below 1 at startup. |
| [args: Add NEGATE_TO_EMPTY so -nofoo reads as an empty string](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/commit/ac4b8feb3fe151d1b00085cfe15a856ccede6e6e) | `GetArg()` returns `"0"` for a negated option. The `-no*notify` options run the command `0`, `-nosigner` uses `0` as signer, `-noi2psam` fails startup and `-norpcpassword` sets the password to `0`. Opt-in because options like `-noonion` and `-noblockfilterindex` depend on reading `"0"`. | New opt-in flag `NEGATE_TO_EMPTY` makes `GetArg()` return `""`. |
| [init: Read -cjdnsreachable and -help as booleans](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/commit/dc4ddbacf791ac6742261bf66dcf42887bfb74ff) | `-cjdnsreachable=0` and `-nocjdnsreachable` turn CJDNS on. `-nohelp` prints the help. | Use `GetBoolArg()` instead of `IsArgSet()`. |
| [args, wallet: Fix empty and negated -blocksdir and -walletdir](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/commit/be71581c2fc65722f6e335e6506cda342eb23ef7) | `-noblocksdir` writes block files relative to the working directory. `-nowalletdir` fails startup. | Fail at startup with `DISALLOW_NEGATION`. An empty value falls back to the default directory, like `-datadir` does. |
| [init: Require -nolistenonion with -notorcontrol](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/commit/44b1c5b05057bf3a768eac63922c085163975dcc) | `-notorcontrol` connects to `0.0.0.0:9051`, which reaches a local Tor. | Fail at startup unless `-listenonion` is disabled. |
| [init: Disallow negating options where it has no meaning](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/commit/6447b07919072f12aba36313814fd4962dd4363a) | `-nocheckblocks`, `-nomaxreceivebuffer`, `-nomaxsendbuffer` and `-nomaxtipage` read as 0, the opposite of what the user asked for. | Fail at startup with `DISALLOW_NEGATION`. |

`-nomempoolexpiry` has a similar kind of problem. It evicts transactions as soon as the next one arrives. I left it out because #36540 already is open and addresses this.

pulls.title: span: diagnose dangling views from MakeByteSpan/MakeUCharSpan
pulls.body:
Follow-up to #36164, as suggested in https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/36164#issuecomment-5541268260.

Tracked in https://github.com/kevkevinpal/bitcoin/issues/550.

Matching the `util/string.h` helpers from #36164.

pulls.title: http: Restore requirement of IPv4 bind success
pulls.body:
### Problem

When bitcoind starts and the HTTP IPv4 listen address is occupied by another process, but the IPv6 address is available, the server fails open and generates a cookie file. When bitcoin-cli runs it picks up the cookie file and sends the credentials in plain text to the non-bitcoind process running on the default IPv4 port. An attacker can then use the credentials to commandeer bitcoind over IPv6.

### Solution

*Safe defaults*:
* When running with default settings, require that the IPv4 bind succeeds.
* When `-rpcbind` is specified, require that all HTTP listen socket binds succeed (fail closed-behavior).

Node operators who only have IPv6 are now required to override `-rpcbind` and `-rpcallowip` to only specify the working interface and allowed subnet if they were not doing so already.

The problem of bitcoin-cli sending the credentials to what could possibly be the wrong process remains **only in non-default setups**.

### History

40b556d3742a1f65d67e2d4c760d0b13fe8be5b7 from 2015 switched the HTTP server from Boost Asio to LibEvent, and binding switched from an attempt at dual-binding IPv4+v6 and falling back to IPv4-only (rpcserver.cpp / `StartRPCThreads()`), to binding IPv4 *or* IPv6 (httpserver.cpp / `HTTPBindAddresses()`). **The current PR restores the prior behavior of IPv4 being mandatory.**

#14968 from 2018 was an attempt to change the behavior to require *all* binds to succeed. But it ran into issues with poor IPv6 support on CI.

### Severity

This credential exfiltration attack requires capability to launch processes on the bitcoind host. If we are on the same account we can already read the cookie credentials off disk. So it's only really interesting when an attacker is on a different user account on the same host.

pulls.title: refactor: Change some validation.cpp methods to return BlockValidationState
pulls.body:
**Summary**. Refactor validation result to be a return value instead of an output parameter in several `validation.cpp` methods.

**Motivation**. The benefits of the change are:
- Exclude the potentially inconsistent case when the bool return value and the returned `state` are inconsistent
- Exclude the ambiguity whether the passed in value of state is used or not (not obvious in chained calls)
- Remove the possibility of unintuitive interaction between subsequent calls with the same state. In case of a validation error, a failure reason is set if the state was valid, but not if it was already invalid.
- Slightly simpler: It's more evident which is the result; one less parameters.

This has grown out from #33856, mentioned in [comment here](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/33856#pullrequestreview-4276791829) and [here](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/33856#issuecomment-4477751949).

**Details**. Many methods follow the scheme where the validation state is returned in an output parameter (`BlockValidationState& state`), and and additional `bool` return value indicating success. In success case the convention is that `state.IsValid()` and the return value are both true. After the change there is only a `BlockValidationState` return value, which is either success (`state.IsValid() == true`), or an invalid/error case.

This change is a highly localized refactor, but touching a sensitive file.

Relevant methods called by `ProcessNewBlockHeaders` and `AcceptBlock` (directly and indirectly) are touched.

Changes are separated into commits by touched methods, ordered by bottom-to-top in the call hierarchy.

pulls.title: descriptor: Represent multipath descriptors in a single Descriptor object
pulls.body:
Currently, multipath descriptor strings treat the multipath specifiers as syntactic sugar. Once we finish parsing such a string, the multipath elements are lost as the result is the multiple distinct descriptors that the multipath is a shorthand for. This means that we are unable to return the multipath string for such descriptors.

This PR allows descriptors to actually be multipath where the multipath specifiers are represented inside of the paths of `BIP32PubkeyProvider`s. This allows for the multipath string to be produced.

In order to achieve this, a lot of derivation path parsing is refactored. `KeyPath` is promoted to being its own class (which subclasses `std::vector`), while the individual derivation indexes become a `KeyPathElement` object so that the multipath elements can be represented. Furthermore, hardened derivation characters are now being stored within `KeyPathElement`s so each element knows what the original hardened character was. This also cleans up a little bit of the descriptor implementation as we no longer have to carry around `bool apostrophe` in a bunch of places.

Lastly, `Parse` now returns a single `Descriptor` object, rather than a vector of them. If the descriptor is a multipath descriptor, the expansion can be retrieved using `GetMultipathExpansion()`. The wallet uses this and still must not store multipath descriptors.

pulls.title: wallet, migration: Skip legacy wallet records rather than erasing them, and drop unused record erase functions
pulls.body: When migrating a legacy wallet, we can skip the records in `MigrateToSQLite` that we would delete later on during migration. These records are specifically all of the legacy wallet records, and transaction records. The legacy wallet records are replaced with descriptor records produced during migration, and transaction records are already being rewritten by migration, so not writing them in the first place is also fine. This allows us to remove several database record erase functions, specifically EraseTx and EraseRecords.

pulls.title: contrib: require trusted signers in verify.py
pulls.body:
`verify_shasums_signature` previously separated signatures into `good_trusted` and `good_untrusted`, but computed `num_trusted = len(good_trusted) + len(good_untrusted)`. As a result, 3 valid signatures from untrusted keys present in the local GPG keyring satisfied `--min-good-sigs` even when none of them were trusted in GPG or matched `--trusted-keys`.

In addition, `README.md` documents passing full 40-character primary key fingerprints to `--trusted-keys`, whereas `parse_gpg_result` only recorded the key identifier from `GOODSIG` and ignored `VALIDSIG` fingerprints, did not deduplicate multiple signatures from the same primary key, and still counted `REVKEYSIG` entries toward the threshold.

Changes:
- Count only distinct, non-revoked trusted signers toward `--min-good-sigs`.
- Parse signing and primary key fingerprints from GnuPG `VALIDSIG` status lines so `--trusted-keys` matches full fingerprints while deduplicating by primary key fingerprint.
- Clarify the trust requirement in `contrib/verify-binaries/README.md`.
- Add unit tests in `contrib/verify-binaries/test.py` (`python3 -m unittest contrib/verify-binaries/test.py -v`).

pulls.title: http: disconnect clients that never finish a request
pulls.body:
The -rpcservertimeout timer only measures inactivity. Every read from a client resets it, so a client that keeps sending bytes without ever completing a request can hold the connection for ever. 

Connection slots are capped by default 16 or by -rpcmaxconnections. Once those slots are taken, the server stops accepting new connections. Because no request ever completes the authentication functions are never hit. 
The impact is low because RPC port binds to localhost by default, so this is a robustness fix rather than a remotely exploitable security issue.

<details> <summary> How to reproduce </summary>

To reproduce: start a node with -rpcmaxconnections=2, open two sockets, and write "GET / HTTP/1.1\r\n" one byte at a time with ten seconds between bytes. bitcoin-cli getblockcount then hangs until one of the (trickling) sockets is closed.

</details>

The fix adds a second deadline next to the idle timer. It is armed on the first byte of a request and expires after -rpcservertimeout (the same value as the idle timer). This timer also does not resets or is extended by later reads. Completing request parsing clears the deadline, so a long-running RPC keeps its connection as before. The deadline is deferred while a worker holds the request, for the same reason the idle timer is. It is restarted while response bytes
are written, because the client cannot start a new request during that window. -rpcservertimeout=0 disables both timers. No new option is added.

Disclaimer this bug is found by utilizing ASTRA. Verified using KIMI 3 and Claude.

pulls.title: contrib: exclude inactive keys from the binary quorum by default
pulls.body:
**Problem:** The binary verifier counts signatures from expired and revoked keys toward `--min-good-sigs`.
Enough of these signatures can satisfy the threshold without any active signing key, and they are returned as good signatures.

**Fix:** Warn about expired and revoked signatures and exclude them from threshold counting by default.
For historical verification, expired signatures can count toward the threshold with `--allow-expired` or `BINVERIFY_ALLOW_EXPIRED`, including signatures created after key expiry. Revoked signatures remain excluded.
Expired signatures are reported separately, including in the `expired_sigs` field in successful JSON output.

The decision uses GnuPG’s current key status from the local keyring, even if the signature was created while the key was active.

This was found and disclosed responsibly by the Red Team 🟥.

pulls.title: wallet: Replace mapWallet and wtxOrdered with a boost::multi_index
pulls.body: The wallet needs to access transactions both by txid, and by insertion order into the wallet. `mapWallet` was the main container for the wallet transactions, and it was keyed by txid. `wtxOrdered` was a secondary container which was keyed by order, and held pointers to the `CWalletTx` objects stored in `mapWallet`. These are replaced by a new boost multi index which indexes on txid and insertion order, allowing us to get rid of the 2 separate containers, and holding raw pointers to `CWalletTx`.

pulls.title: rpc: Manual prune lock management (Take 2)
pulls.body:
This is a refreshed version of #19463, which was closed due to inactivity.

Motivation: On pruned nodes, if a wallet is not loaded while the node is running, blocks necessary for rescanning when the wallet is loaded may be pruned. This PR allows users and external wallet software to manually manage prune locks via RPC, so they can protect blocks needed for future rescans and also clean up locks that are no longer relevant (e.g. after permanently unloading a wallet from a node). This is useful both for Bitcoin Core's own wallet and for external wallets that use Bitcoin Core as a backend. Usage of temporary prune locking may also be helpful in other functional test scenarios but I didn't spend time to check where might apply.

This PR leverages the existing prune locks system we already have. The interface of the RPCs of the old PR has been slightly updated, it now matches the pattern used by `setban`/`listbanned` exactly. The locks are prefixed to distinguish them from the systems locks and prevent naming colissions. They are not persisted across restarts.

pulls.title: Add output script index and corresponding script history RPC
pulls.body:
Add a new index `txoscriptindex` which indexes all output scripts. Introduce a new `getscripthistory` RPC that returns all transactions that create outputs corresponding to the provided scripts, and optionally the transactions that spend those outputs if `txospenderindex` is also configured.

This has been a long-requested feature, attempted in previous PRs (#2802, #3652, #6835, #10370, #14053).
Some concerns raised were about the ability for an index like this to scale. I think the new techniques being used to build the indexes (https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/35531, https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/36002) alleviate this concern. This index can be synced in a few hours and the current disk usage is ~54 GB. This is less than the ~66 GB `txindex` disk usage in v31 and earlier. This index can also be used with a pruned node, so a full node can be supported in < 100 GB of disk space. Missing blocks are returned by hash and can be requested from peers using `getblockfrompeer`.

Some other previous concerns were more conceptual, that this type of index could encourage address reuse and chain analysis. IMO this ship has sailed, and the current status quo of not shipping an address index is turning off users who expect this functionality. Workarounds involve installing, configuring, and syncing other third-party software, making the UX of using Bitcoin Core in a self-sovereign way unnecessarily difficult.

The index hashes each output script with SHA256, then applies salted SipHash-1-3-UJ and stores a six-byte prefix. This is to support the popular Electrum protocol, which supplies only the script hash. The RPC can also look up by address or descriptors. Ranged descriptors are also supported, so a single RPC call can return the entire history of a receive/change xpub pair.

Because there are some scripts with millions of outputs, we introduce a new `OrderedVarInt` which serializes the block height after the script hash prefix. This lets LevelDB seek directly to the prefix + block height, so we can page by block height range.

To prevent DoS concerns by supplying an address with millions of outputs, the RPC tracks a byte budget of reads and throws immediately if too many reads are attempted. The error message instructs the user to narrow the block range.

Improvements to `txospenderindex` (https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/36480) will also allow us to use that pruned. The end result would allow users to run with all optional indexes (including this one) in < 200 GB of disk space. Of course a larger pruned setting would be desired if many historical block lookups were being requested.

pulls.title: rpc: report background validation progress in getchainstates
pulls.body:
After #33259, `getblockchaininfo` reports the progress of the background chainstate relative to the snapshot base block, but `getchainstates` still computes `verificationprogress` against the network tip for every chainstate, so the same node reports two different numbers for the same chainstate.

This PR modifies `verificationprogress` value to report the correct value, relative to the block the chainstate actually stops at.

pulls.title: test: fuzz: check CoinGrinder completed flag
HTTPServer: Prevent race condition between worker thread and I/O thread
pulls.body:
This prevents a losing race condition that could prevent the server from reading any more requests from an HTTP client.

Found and reported by the fuzzing department: https://github.com/dergoegge/bitcoin/commit/7fe5f54497c86f216b619e340939447504e87dcb

The Race:

A connected socket can either be written to or read from based on the result of `GenerateWaitSockets()`. That method checks the `HTTPRemoteClient` flag `m_send_ready`. If it's `true` the implication is that there is data in the client's send buffer ready to go. Once that data is sent and the buffer is empty, `MaybeSendBytesFromBuffer()` sets it `false` again.

The sad case was when a worker thread calling `WriteReply()` adds data to the send buffer, but before it sets `m_send_ready` to `true`, the I/O thread sends that data and empties the buffer. With the buffer unexpectedly empty, `WriteReply()` sets `m_send_ready` to `true`.

The effect of this is that the socket will stay in "write" mode with nothing to write. With nothing to write, `MaybeSendBytesFromBuffer()` never sets it back to `false` and the socket is stuck forever.

The Fix:

Simply move `m_send_ready = true` inside the block of `WriteReply()` where `m_send_mutex` is still held. This prevents the I/O thread from emptying the send buffer while the worker thread is setting the flag.

Testing:

To observe the race condition, revert the first commit `"http: prevent race condition between worker thread and I/O thread"` and run the unit test from the  remainder of the branch. I like to see the logs:

`test_bitcoin --log_level=all  --run_test=httpserver_tests -- --printtoconsole --debug=http --debug=lock'

The test will fail with a small probability. The socket will get stuck and the test will abort after a 60 second timeout. To garuntee the race condition loses and fail the test every time, slow down `WriteReply()` in the worker thread:

```diff
diff --git a/src/httpserver.cpp b/src/httpserver.cpp
index 99e30ff663..b0c7b516d8 100644
--- a/src/httpserver.cpp
+++ b/src/httpserver.cpp
@@ -614,6 +614,7 @@ void HTTPRequest::WriteReply(HTTPStatusCode status, std::span<const std::byte> r
     } else {
         // Inform HTTPServer I/O that data is ready to be sent to this client
         // in the next loop iteration.
+        std::this_thread::sleep_for(500ms);
         m_client->m_send_ready = true;
     }
 
```

With the first commit (the fix) back in place, slowing down the worker thread like this won't fail the test.

Bonus:

The unit test is spread over three commits. First, a method of the socket testing setup is templated so a mock socket that intentionally raises an error can be inserted. The unit test added in that commit covers a race condition that was fixed in #35182 in response to https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/35182/changes#r3358889539 so we get the added benefit of covering an error path, and guaranteeing coverage of both "optimistic send" (directly from worker thread) and regular send (from a tick in the I/O loop thread).

The next commit adds a worker thread to the unit test, at which point a race condition is possible but very unlikely because all requests are sent at once. Finally, we spread out the requests in the top commit and make the race condition much easier to catch.

pulls.title: rpc: Let dumptxoutset fail early on stale targets and concurrent runs
pulls.body:
This improves handling of two edge cases where `dumptxoutset` currently only fails after doing unnecessary and possibly incorrect work:

Stale rollback target (first commit): `ParseHashOrHeight` accepts any known block hash, and the rollback path never checks the target is on the active chain. The full UTXO set is copied and blocks are disconnected back from the tip only to fail when the target block height is reached. This is now rejected before all that as an invalid param, matching the check in `getchaintxstats` and `scanblocks`. This is a pretty unlikely scenario but the fix is also very small.

Concurrent calls (second commit): Nothing prevented triggering two runs at once and since this is a relatively long running operation I don't think it is that unlikely that this might happen by accident or that users think this might actually be a possible thing to do if you want two different dumps. On master currently both runs would write to `<path>.incomplete`, so the second dump to the same path corrupts the file the first one reports as successfully written. And also the prune lock has a fixed name, so the second run overwrites the first's height and the first to finish deletes the others lock mid-rollback. A second call now fails immediately with "dumptxoutset is already running". `TemporaryPruneLock` is extended and renamed to `DumptxoutsetGuard` and handles both the general running of multiple instances and the lock management. The alternative to this approach would be to allow for concurrent runs and fix that behavior but it seemed to me like that would be overengineering considering that the audience for this functionality should be very small.

pulls.title: RFC: netbase: Remove manual_connection and return the failure reason to callers
pulls.body:
Based on #36969, only the last commit is new. Draft to see if this direction is wanted. This also came out of discussions in #36759: 

The `manual_connection` flag of `ConnectDirectly()` only picks the log level of a failed `connect()`. Callers that are not manual peers, like Tor control, pass `true` just to get the failure logged, and the caller that knows how much a failure matters never sees the reason.

This removes the flag. `ConnectDirectly()` returns the failure reason and each caller decides how to log it. The log output stays the same, except that manual peers and Tor control now log every failure reason at info level, including timeouts, which were debug only.

**Summary:** This PR contains a few different optimizations found by IBD profiling and via the newly added block serialization benchmarks. It also takes advantage of the recently merged [`std::span` changes](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/31519) enabling propagating static extents.

pulls.title: validation: throw when a compressed script can't be decompressed
pulls.body:
`ScriptCompression::Unser` ignores the `DecompressScript` return value and
leaves the script empty on failure, without notifying upper layers about the error.
In the worst-case scenario, which is currently only reachable through corruption,
an unspendable off-curve P2PK turns into an anyone-can-spend empty script.
Given that, properly throwing the error to prevent any future mistakes from
happening seems the sanest path to follow.

Aside from that, added coverage for a P2PK script with an uncompressed pubkey
that has a valid X but a wrong Y, which makes it unspendable. Checking we store
such scripts raw and never encode them as 0x04/0x05, as those encodings
serialize X with only Y's parity (not the full Y), which would make decompression
recompute Y from X and turn the unspendable script into a spendable one, which
would not be good.

pulls.title: test/mutation: check wallet listings and wrapped P2WSH addresses in `wallet_migration.py`
pulls.body:
**Problem:** The migration test checks the legacy-wallet warning only if it finds the wallet in `listwalletdir`, so a missing wallet goes unnoticed.
It skips the warning check for `path/to/trailing/` even when the wallet is listed because the returned name has no trailing separator.
After migration, the test looks for a dictionary containing only the backup name, but every entry also has a `warnings` field, so the check passes even if the backup is listed.

The P2WSH test imports a wrapped output but checks only the native address after migration.

**Fix:** Require `listwalletdir` to return the legacy wallet with its migration warning, then check that the backup filename is absent from the listed names after migration.
For both the native and wrapped addresses, check that `getaddressinfo` reports `ismine` as true and includes the `embedded` field.

**Mutation tests:** To test each change, apply the mutation in its commit message and run `wallet_migration.py`.

pulls.title: blockstorage: fix partial-mask assertions and genesis availability checks
pulls.body:
**Problem:** `CheckBlockDataAvailability` checks whether the upper block has any requested bit. `GetFirstBlock` requires every requested bit, so a partial match can reach its assertion. At genesis, the existing undo exception can reject an undo-only request or accept a request with missing block data. It also misses ranges containing only genesis.

**Fix:** Require every requested bit on each block in the range, except that genesis needs no undo data. An empty mask now succeeds for a valid range because it requests no bits. Both index-startup calls supply nonempty masks.

pulls.title: wallet: Track no-longer-spendable TXOs separately
pulls.body:
In #27286, the wallet keeps track of all of its transaction outputs, even if they are already spent or are otherwise unspendable. This TXO set is iterated for balance checking and coin selection preparation, which can still be slow for wallets that have had a lot of activity. This PR aims to improve the performance of such wallets by moving UTXOs that are definitely no longer spendable to a different map in the wallet so that far fewer TXOs need to be iterated for the aforementioned functions.

Unspendable TXOs (not to be confused with Unspent TXOs) are those which have a spending transaction that has been confirmed, or are no longer valid due to reorgs. TXOs that are spent in unconfirmed transactions remain in the primary TXO set, and are filtered out of balance and coin selection as before.

pulls.title: wallet: Fix detection of symlinks on Windows
pulls.body:
This PR implements symlink detection for Windows, since GCC [doesn't support symlinks on Windows](https://gcc.gnu.org/git/?p=gcc.git;a=blob;f=libstdc%2B%2B-v3/src/filesystem/ops-common.h;h=ba377905a2e90f7baf30c900b090f1f732397e08;hb=refs/heads/releases/gcc-13#l124). This is used by the wallet's `ListDatabases` in order to detect symlinks and avoid recursing them. It's also used in wallet path validation since that is also checking whether paths are symlinks, and we should properly detect symlinks on Windows.

Under the hood, the `IsSymlink` function uses `std::filesystem::is_symlink` for non-Windows systems. On Windows, it checks a file's attributes to determine if it is a [reparse point](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/fileio/reparse-points). Strictly speaking, this will also catch files that aren't symlinks, such as directories that are Onedrive mounts. I think it's fine to not be recursively searching such directories.

This is based on #34418 for the multiwallet test and CI changes that it enables. The last commit also removes the skipping of the symlink checks so that we are testing that the symlink handling behavior on Windows matches that on Linux and MacOS.

pulls.title: wallet, refactor: modularise wallet by extracting out legacy wallet migration
pulls.body:
I've been meaning to scratch this itch for quite some time. It has been noted
by many developers that the `wallet/wallet.cpp` file is quite hard to reason
about.

It is more than 4500 lines long currently and this patch is an attempt to
shortern it by around 800 lines by extracting out the wallet migration code into
a dedicated `wallet/migration.cpp` file.

The other benefits of this PR I see are that it moves the legacy wallet stuff
from the main wallet file that paves the way for it being descriptor specific
(as much as possible), and makes legacy wallet migration code a first-class
citizen in its own file.

I hope it makes it easier for everyone to go through the main wallet file.

This patchset **should** be reviewed with --color-moved=dimmed-zebra option.

pulls.title: sign: Remove FillableSigningProvider
pulls.body:
`FillableSigningProvider` was initially extracted from the wallet in order to produce the `SigningProvider` encapsulation system that we use today for the wallet and for providing key material to signing. It's primary user was the legacy wallet, but it was also being used as a convenience in a few other places. Since the legacy wallet is removed, there is no need to keep it around as a separate class. Instead, the things that it was doing can be inlined into `LegacyDataSPKM` where the functionality is actually being used to support migrating legacy wallets.

The remaining uses are tests and the `bitcoin-tx` tool, some of which were relying on the implicit addition of segwit scripts when adding a key. However, these can also use `FlatSigningProvider` with explicitly adding the segwit scripts when necessary, and have thusly been converted to do so.

pulls.title: refactor: extract per-message helpers from ProcessMessage (move-only)
pulls.body:
`PeerManagerImpl::ProcessMessage()` is a ~1500-line function handling every p2p message type inline, which makes it hard to navigate and review.

This PR continues splitting it into per-message helper functions, following the pattern of the recently merged fa5ab0220e02377c3c855042ecdf1f5f950d0965 (`ProcessPong()`) and fa55723b8fbd4fd056dddac5b35daf2e86021422 (`ProcessAddrs()`), as suggested by maflcko https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/34588#issuecomment-4658892004.

A preparatory commit removes the `__func__` prefix from one getheaders debug log, so moving it doesn't change the output.

Nine handlers are extracted, one move-only commit each:

  * `ProcessGetAddr()` — `getaddr`
  * `ProcessGetDataMessage()` — `getdata` (named to avoid colliding with the existing `ProcessGetData()`, which services the request queue this handler fills)
  * `ProcessGetBlocks()` — `getblocks`
  * `ProcessGetHeaders()` — `getheaders`
  * `ProcessInv()` — `inv`
  * `ProcessSendTxRcncl()` — `sendtxrcncl`
  * `ProcessTx()` — `tx`
  * `ProcessCompactBlock()` — `cmpctblock`
  * `ProcessVersion()` — `version`

Each extraction commit is a code move with indentation adjustments: the only new lines are the declaration (with thread-safety annotations), the function signature, and the one-line call site.
Each call site is `Helper(...); return;`, so `return` statements inside the moved bodies keep identical semantics. No behavior change beyond debug log output.

One final cleanup commit normalizes the remaining formatting, replaces equivalent `break` statements with `return` in `ProcessSendTxRcncl()`, and simplifies the `send_getaddr` conditional in `ProcessVersion()`.

Each extraction commit can be reviewed with the git options:
`--color-moved=dimmed-zebra --color-moved-ws=ignore-all-space`

Declarations and definitions are placed next to related existing helpers (e.g. `ProcessGetDataMessage` next to `ProcessGetData`, `ProcessGetBlocks` next to `ProcessGetBlockData`, `ProcessGetAddr` after `ProcessAddrs`).

pulls.title: test: make `tx_mempool_block_doublespend` cases independent
pulls.body:
Found during #36692: remove test state that is shared and modified across cases.

`tx_mempool_block_doublespend` ran four cases against one chain and mempool, removing each case’s mempool transaction by hand before the next one. Each case is now its own test with a fresh setup that builds the two spends. The first commit also fixes the last case’s comment, which had the mempool and block spends reversed. The checks are unchanged.

The second commit makes the two spends distinct transactions. Previously they were identical (deterministic signing), so in the last case the mempool transaction was removed because it was mined rather than as a conflict. The rejection cases are unaffected: they fail with `bad-txns-inputs-missingorspent` either way.

pulls.title: log: Remove trailing and embedded newlines from log messages
pulls.body:
The log functions sometimes have a trailing newline character. This is perfectly fine, because that char will be stripped again by the log framework. However, it is still confusing:

* After https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/35833 *embedded* newlines are escaped and a single trailing one is excluded. It would be clearer to not have a special carve-out here. Also the carve-out may be missing two-or-more trailing newlines.
* The trailing newline may incorrectly imply that newlines are supported at all.

So remove them, and also fix a few places to remove embedded newlines.

pulls.title: kernel: Use typed errors for fatal and flush error notifications
pulls.body:
Part of the libbitcoinkernel project (tracking issue #27587 ), specifically the "Remove translation.h usage from the kernel" item. `kernel::Notifications::fatalError()` and `flushError()` take a `bilingual_str`, which pulls `util/translation.h` and the application-level `G_TRANSLATION_FUN` into the kernel library, and translation is an application concern rather than a consensus one. The same interface already shows the way out: `warningSet()` takes a `kernel::Warning` enum, and the node turns it into a translated string in `node/kernel_notifications.cpp`.

Along with removing the dependency, another goal here is separating responsibilities, because the goals of error handling and error reporting are different: presenting an error to a user is an application concern, not something `libbitcoinkernel` itself should own. The error is structured on both sides: in C++ as the full `kernel::FatalError` variant, and in the C API as its numeric value. With the current changes the C side only carries half of that structure today though, the dynamic fields (a block hash, a path, an exception's `what()`) do not cross the C API yet, even though ideally they should.

This PR does the same for the two error notifications. A new `src/kernel/error.h` defines `kernel::FlushError` as a plain enum and `kernel::FatalError` as a `std::variant` with one struct per error, whose fields carry the context the message needs: a block hash, a path, the `what()` of a caught exception, block heights. It holds types and nothing else, so every message is now built on the node side. The exception is `FatalErrorString()` in `validation.cpp`, because a fatal error raised during validation also fails the block through `BlockValidationState::Error()`, which takes the reason as a plain string right there, and `fatalError()` returns void, so the node has no way to put its message into that state. A follow-up could store the typed error in the state instead and let the node create the string message.

This does not remove the kernel's dependency on `util/translation.h`, it is just a step. The other two notifications, `progress()` and `warningSet()`, still take a `bilingual_str`, and `bitcoinkernel.cpp`, `checks.cpp`, `node/chainstate.cpp`, `txmempool.cpp` and `validation.cpp` still include the header.

There is one behavior change to mention here. The two C API callbacks lose their `message` parameter, so they now carry only the error code, the same pattern that `btck_BlockValidationResult` already uses.

pulls.title: net: only monitor select exceptions while connecting
pulls.body:
Alternative approach to #36688, citing the relevant parts of its description:

> There is currently nothing preventing us to receive TCP urgent data, which would never be returned by `recv()`. Linux's `poll()` is indifferent to this, but the `select()` socket monitoring may keep reporting it as pending on some platforms.
>
> This would not prevent progress nor lead to a crash anymore after #36665, but it's still undesirable.

Fix this by only adding a socket to the `select()` exception set while waiting for a non-blocking `connect()` to complete. Windows needs that to detect a failed connection. Established connections no longer monitor the exception set on any platform. This approach was suggested by theuni in https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/36716#issuecomment-6931290348 and replaces the earlier version of this PR, which ignored the exception set outside Windows and disconnected on it on Windows.

We could instead have set `SO_OOBINLINE` on our sockets, so `recv()` returns any urgent data sent to us (and likely leads us to disconnect the peer). RFC 6093 doesn't forbid this, but the current approach seems more clear and direct to me.

A new unit test in `sock_tests` covers the fix itself: with an urgent byte pending, waiting for `RecvEvent` must time out. Without the fix it fails on a `select()` build. The mock sockets in `src/test/util/net.cpp` and `src/test/fuzz/util/net.cpp` no longer report the new flag as an occurred event.

Backports until 29.x are straight-forward, but for 31.x and before require compensating for the scripted-diff in https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/commit/f395acdeeeaa1f3fd75d3cedbf2731fa24083e9f.

pulls.body:

pulls.title: streams: handle buffered write failures outside the destructor
pulls.body:
**Problem:** Block and undo writers buffer serialized data, then rely on the `BufferedWriter` destructor to write the remaining bytes.
`fwrite()` can report fewer bytes written than requested after a local storage error, e.g., if the filesystem fills up while a block is being written (my 1 TB benchmarking servers have recently been filling up, so I've been seeing these failures more often).
`AutoFile::write_buffer()` converts that result into an exception, and because the destructor is implicitly non-throwing, the exception invokes `std::terminate`.
Calling `flush()` before destruction is insufficient on its own because a failed flush leaves the same bytes pending, so the destructor retries the write while the original exception unwinds.

I introduced this bug in #31551 when adding `BufferedWriter`.

I’d update the **Fix** section to include `discard()` and describe exactly what the destructor checks. The problem statement and reproducer can stay as written.

**Fix:** Block and undo writers now flush explicitly before destruction.
If serialization or writing throws `std::ios_base::failure`, they discard any pending bytes, log the error, close the file, and request shutdown through the existing fatal-error path.
`BufferedWriter` clears the pending byte count before writing because the stream may obfuscate the bytes in place and a short write may already have put some of them on disk, making a retry unsafe.
The destructor uses `Assume` to check that no bytes are pending before attempting a fallback flush.
`flush()` continues to propagate exceptions, and `AutoFile` remains unchanged.

<details>
<summary>Manual write-error reproducer</summary>

Force the error path in `AutoFile::write_buffer()`:

```sh
sed -i '' '/^.*AutoFile::write_buffer(/,/^}/s/!= src.size()/!= 0/' src/streams.cpp
cmake -B build && cmake --build build -j5 && build/bin/bitcoind -regtest -datadir="$(mktemp -d)"; echo "exit=$?"
```

Before this change, implicit flushing invokes `std::terminate`:

> libc++abi: terminating due to uncaught exception of type std::__1::ios_base::failure: AutoFile::write_buffer: write failed: unspecified iostream_category error
> zsh: abort      build/bin/bitcoind -regtest -datadir="$(mktemp -d)"
> exit=134

With this change, `bitcoind` logs the write failure, then completes normal shutdown and exits with status 1:

> Checking all blk files are present...
> [error] Failed to write block file FlatFilePos(nFile=0, nPos=8): AutoFile::write_buffer: write failed: unspecified iostream_category error
> ...
> Error: A fatal internal error occurred, see debug.log for details: Failed to write block.
> [error] Writing genesis block to disk failed
> [error] Error initializing block database
> ...
> Shutdown done
> exit=1
</details>

pulls.title: RFC: consensus: Make `CAmount` a class
pulls.body:
We should treat people's money with care across node and wallet.

Having our `CAmount` be a `typedef` for raw `int64_t` as on master has the following drawbacks:
* Allows assigning to from `bool`s, leading to the issues like the one previously fixed by 0026b330c4abbbbdb96e4f0c4d380d70d8e592ab.
* Allows direct comparison with integral types of differing size, leading to things like the issue previously fixed by 890a09b1e49925315a5636f29cc5af36928fe092 (reverting it on top of this PR leads to compile errors).
* Allows forgetting to initialize amounts (`CAmount fee;`).
* Allows direct operations with imprecise decimal types as in `CAmount target = 49.5L * COIN` in src/wallet/test/coinselector_tests.cpp.
* Allows *multiplying* two `CAmount`s with each other, which does not make sense.

Beyond fixing the above, this PR also makes amounts stick out more in code - either by the `CAmount` type itself or by using the `sats` unit specifier.

This work is also a stepping stone for possible future work introducing an even safer amount type which only allows values in the range `[0, MAX_MONEY]`.

Already merged PRs spawned out of this work: #35456, #35372

Prior attempts in similar directions: #5430, #4067

pulls.title: psbt: verify final scripts in FinalizePSBT
pulls.body:
`finalizepsbt` can return `complete: true` and a hex for a PSBT whose `PSBT_IN_FINAL_SCRIPTWITNESS` (or final scriptSig) is invalid.

`FinalizePSBT` counts an input as complete when `SignPSBTInput` succeeds. If the input already has final fields, `PSBTInput::FillSignatureData` marks the sigdata complete and `ProduceSignature` returns true early (sign.cpp:752), before the script is verified. So the existing final fields are trusted as-is.

To reproduce, take a signed P2WPKH v0 PSBT that has a `non_witness_utxo` and flip one bit of the signature inside the final witness:
- `finalizepsbt` returns `complete: true` and a hex
- `analyzepsbt` says the input is not final, `next: finalizer`
- `testmempoolaccept` on the hex fails with `mempool-script-verify-flag-failed (Signature must be zero for failed CHECK(MULTI)SIG operation)`

Inputs that only have a `witness_utxo` already come out incomplete because of the `require_witness_sig` check, so this affects inputs with a `non_witness_utxo`.

#30357 fixed the same problem in `FillPSBT` by checking `PSBTInputSignedAndVerified`, and #33014 did it for `descriptorprocesspsbt`. This does the same in `FinalizePSBT`. Taproot verification needs every spent output. If one is missing, that input already fails in `SignPSBTInput` with `MISSING_INPUTS` and makes the PSBT incomplete, so the extra check doesn't change the result in that case.

The new test in `rpc_psbt.py` builds that PSBT and checks that `finalizepsbt` returns `complete: false` with no hex. It fails on master and passes with the fix. `wallet_musig.py` and the `psbt_wallet_tests` / `script_tests` unit tests still pass.

One behaviour change: a final script that is valid by consensus but non-standard now gives `complete: false`. `FillPSBT` and `descriptorprocesspsbt` already behave that way, since they check with the same standard flags.

pulls.title: validation: don't accept txs to the mempool while loading a snapshot
pulls.body:
`ActivateSnapshot` checks that the mempool is empty before it starts, but `PopulateAndValidateSnapshot` then runs without `cs_main`, which takes minutes on mainnet. A transaction entering the mempool in that window (e.g. through `sendrawtransaction`) hits the assert in `AddChainstate`:

```
Assertion failed: (!prev_chainstate.m_mempool || prev_chainstate.m_mempool->size() == 0), function AddChainstate, file validation.cpp, line 6201.
```

By then the base blockhash file has been written, so the node needs `-reindex` to start again.

This sets a flag on `ChainstateManager` while `ActivateSnapshot` runs, and `AcceptToMemoryPool` and `ProcessNewPackage` reject with `snapshot-loading` while it's set. `testmempoolaccept` still works. A second `loadtxoutset` started while one is running is also rejected.

`test_mempool_blocked_during_load` in `feature_assumeutxo.py` pauses the load through a FIFO, checks that `sendrawtransaction` and `submitpackage` are rejected and the mempool stays empty, then lets the load finish. On master the transaction is accepted and the node aborts. The test is skipped where `os.mkfifo` isn't available.

pulls.title: net: limit relative ban times to uint32
pulls.body:
`BanMan::Ban` computes the ban end as `GetTime() + bantime` (banman.cpp:140). `setban` and `-bantime` both accept any int64, so a relative bantime close to `INT64_MAX`:

```
setban 1.2.3.5 add 9223372036854775807
```

returns success, but the sum overflows. UBSan reports:

```
src/banman.cpp:140:73: runtime error: signed integer overflow: 1790412558 + 9223372036854775807 cannot be represented in type 'int64_t'
```

Without UBSan the result wraps negative, the ban is treated as already expired, and it is silently dropped. With `-bantime=9223372036854775807` the same happens to every `setban add` that uses the default duration.

This limits relative ban times to uint32 (about 136 years):

- `setban` rejects a relative bantime above `UINT32_MAX` with "Error: bantime is too large"
- `-bantime` is parsed as `uint32_t`, so larger values saturate at `UINT32_MAX`

Absolute timestamps are unchanged.

The added cases in `rpc_setban.py` check that `UINT32_MAX + 1` and `INT64_MAX` are rejected, that `UINT32_MAX` is accepted, and that with `-bantime=INT64_MAX` a default-duration ban is listed with a duration of `UINT32_MAX`. Both parts fail on master and pass with the change. `p2p_disconnect_ban.py` still passes.

AI tools were used to help find this issue and to prepare the patch and test.
