pulls.title: Configuration argument handling improvements.
pulls.body:
Several numeric configuration options now reject values that are out of range instead of silently wrapping or inverting. Previously a negative value could disable the intended limit entirely.

  - `-dbbatchsize` and `-dbcrashratio` must be non-negative. A negative `-dbbatchsize` wrapped to a huge value and disabled batch flushing, so a reindex could hold an unbounded batch in memory.
  - `-limitclustersize`, `-limitancestorcount`, `-limitdescendantcount`, `-mempoolexpiry`, `-datacarriersize`, `-maxsendbuffer`, `-maxreceivebuffer`, `-bantime`, `-bytespersigop` and `-maxtipage` must be non-negative.
  - `-limitclustercount` must be between 1 and 64.
  - `-timeout` must be positive. It previously fell back to the default silently, unlike the analogous `-peertimeout`, which already errored.

  Zero remains valid wherever it already meant "disabled": `-dbbatchsize=0`,
  `-limitclustersize=0`, `-datacarriersize=0`, `-mempoolexpiry=0`,
  `-maxtipage=0`, `-bytespersigop=0`, `-maxsendbuffer=0`,
  `-maxreceivebuffer=0` and `-bantime=0`.

- The `-help` output for `-bytespersigop`, `-datacarriersize`, `-dbbatchsize`, `-stopatheight` and `-checkblockindex` now shows the `=<n>` placeholder for their value, matching how they are actually parsed.

pulls.title: p2p: replace full outbound peers that don't support tx relay (take 2)
pulls.body:
Picks up #28538

Outbound-full-relay slots should be used by peers that actually relay transactions, besides #28538 see #16418 and #28371 for the motivation. So try to replace peers that are not relaying txs with peers that do.

The approach differs from the original PR in a few details in response to some of the review comments there:

- A replacement is connected before the peer is evicted. The original PR disconnected a non-tx-relaying peer once all full outbound slots were filled. Reviewers preferred having a replacement available first (https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/28538#issuecomment-1883481846). Now an extra outbound-full-relay connection is requested, like the extra network-specific peers, and the existing eviction of extra outbound peers prefers peers that don't relay txs.
- Peers not relaying txs don't get `m_protect`. Otherwise they could stay forever (https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/28538#discussion_r1443336121), and ignoring the protection was rejected in the same thread (https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/28538#discussion_r1443312604).
- An only peer on a network is not replaced. Otherwise the network-specific extra connections and this logic would keep replacing each other (https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/28538#issuecomment-1883481846). This also covers the `-maxconnections=1` case (https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/28538#discussion_r1417178196).

Nothing is changed in `-blocksonly` mode or during IBD. The rename commit and the functional test are taken from the original PR with some changes to match the new behavior.

pulls.title: wallet, bdbro: Reject overflow pages without data
pulls.body:
`BerkeleyRODatabase::Open` reads an overflow record by following `next_page` until it is 0. #34959 added a check that stops once more data than `item_len` was read, which needs every page to add data. An overflow page with `hf_offset` 0 adds none. If such a page names itself as `next_page`, the loop reads it again and again and never ends.

This PR treats an overflow page without data as corruption.

**Behavior change:** a file with an empty overflow page no longer opens and fails with `Overflow page has no data`. Before, an empty page with `next_page` 0 was accepted and the record came out shorter than `item_len`.

**Measurement:** regtest, RelWithDebInfo, base a527a0077a. The file has 5 pages of 4096 bytes: one key whose value is an overflow record with `item_len` 100, and one overflow page.

| overflow page | master | this PR |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `hf_offset` 0, `next_page` itself | `bitcoin-wallet dump` at 100 % of one core, killed after 60 s | fails at once, exit 1 |
| `hf_offset` 100, `next_page` 0 | dumped in 0.11 s | dumped as before |

With `migratewallet` on master the RPC does not return and one HTTP worker stays at 100 % CPU. Other RPCs still answer, but `stop` had not finished after 30 s.

**Tests:** new case in `tool_wallet.py` that writes both files by hand. On master it hangs (killed after 90 s). Passing locally: `test_bitcoin` and `test_runner.py` with the default list. Not run: fuzz targets, lint.

Contributed by [turingpoint](https://www.turingpoint.de).

pulls.title: compressor: oversized script decoding can leave a spendable script
pulls.body:
**Problem:** The oversized-script fallback appends `OP_RETURN` to the destination instead of replacing it. If the destination already contains an unfinished push, the appended byte becomes pushed data and the result can remain spendable.

**Fix:** Replace the destination with `OP_RETURN` rather than appending it.

Found while reviewing #36280. This predates that PR and appears latent because oversized outputs are excluded from the UTXO set, but it could affect malformed stored records decoded into a reused destination.

pulls.title: test: avoid BSD ephemeral-port collisions in HTTP clients
pulls.body:
While stress-testing #36147 I noticed sporadic port collisions still occurring on FreeBSD.

`set_ephemeral_port_range()` keeps the source port out of the test port range, but only for sockets the framework creates itself. Python's `http.client` creates its sockets internally, so RPC and REST connections can still be given a source port inside the test range. A connection to a closed port can then connect to itself. For example, the wrong-RPC-port startup check failed with `BadStatusLine: POST / HTTP/1.1` because the client read back its own request.

This change adds a `netutil.HTTPConnection` subclass that sets the port range before connecting, and uses it in `AuthServiceProxy` and in the tests that open HTTP connections directly.

HTTPS is left unchanged because we don't serve RPC over TLS so it seems unnecessary.

pulls.title: guix: compute --build triplet when lowering, not at load time
pulls.body:
### Why

`building-on` in `contrib/guix/toolchains.scm` reads `(%current-system)` once, when the module is loaded. `guix shell` loads the manifest before it applies `--system`, so the value is the system of the machine that runs the build, not the system that Guix builds for.

So a build with `ADDITIONAL_GUIX_ENVIRONMENT_FLAGS="--system=aarch64-linux"` on an x86_64 machine (for example with `qemu-binfmt-service-type`, to get an aarch64 build machine) configures the aarch64 cross toolchain with `--build=x86_64-guix-linux-gnu`. `gcc-cross-sans-libc` then fails to configure:

```
checking for CET support... configure: error: compiler and assembler with CET support are required for --enable-cet
```

### What changes

`building-on` becomes a procedure, and its three call sites call it. Guix then computes the triplet for each derivation, under the system that the derivation is built for.

### How I checked

- On master, `HOST=x86_64-linux-gnu guix shell -n --system=aarch64-linux -m contrib/guix/linux_static.scm` (with `toolchains.scm` on the load path, as `guix-build` does) gives `gcc-cross-sans-libc` with `--build=x86_64-guix-linux-gnu`. With this PR it gives `--build=aarch64-guix-linux-gnu`. That is the same derivation that `guix build -d --system=aarch64-linux` gives on master.
- Native builds (no `--system`): the toolchain derivations from `linux_static.scm` and `manifest_gui.scm` are identical on master and with this PR. So this PR does not change release builds.
- With this PR, an emulated aarch64 build of `x86_64-linux-gnu` on x86_64 built the whole cross toolchain and the non-GUI binaries. The GUI environment then failed in the tests of `python-pylint` (timeout under emulation) and `maturin` (snapshot mismatch). These packages have no aarch64 substitutes at the pinned Guix commit, and the failures are not related to this change.

pulls.title: txindex: allow running in pruned mode
pulls.body:
After #35531, each txindex entry now points to the block hash containing the tx instead of the file location of the block. The block hash is then used to find the file position of the block to read the tx from. This allows us to determine the hash of the containing block even if the block is later pruned, and also determine the location of the block on disk if it is later downloaded again via `getblockfrompeer`.

This PR enables maintaining a txindex while pruned. If a txid lookup tries to read a tx from a pruned block, the hash of the missing block is surfaced to the caller.

If desired, a user may call `getblockfrompeer` using the returned hash to download the block, then try again successfully. The downloaded block will be added to the front of the block queue, so won't be pruned again for at least 288 blocks. Of course a larger prune setting is desired if lots of historical blocks will be read, and there are privacy issues if the user is looking up their own transactions. Ideally the blocks can be fetched from a trusted node or from random peers with decoy blocks fetched occasionally.

Resolves https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/10609, https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/12651, https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/16182, https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/35240

pulls.title: ipc: Expose Chain interface to IPC clients
pulls.body:
**Problem:** Processes connected to `bitcoin-node` over IPC (with `-ipcbind`) can use the `Mining` interface, but they can't currently use the `Chain` interface to read chain data or follow chain events. Chain data could be useful to third-party clients and Bitcoin Core's own wallet could use this as well to run in a separate process (#10102). But exposing all of `interfaces::Chain` to external clients would make its methods hard to change, since the wallet uses them as internal API (#34981).

**Solution:** Add capnp wrappers for `interfaces::Chain`, split into two interfaces backed by the same C++ class:

- `Chain`, returned by `Init.makeChain`, is stable. It follows Cap'n Proto schema evolution rules, so existing clients keep working as methods are added. It starts with the five block lookup methods: `findBlock`, `findFirstBlockWithTimeAndHeight`, `findAncestorByHeight`, `findAncestorByHash` and `findCommonAncestor`.
- `UnstableChain`, returned by `Init.makeUnstableChain`, extends `Chain` with every other method, for Bitcoin Core's internal C++ callers, such as the wallet, communicating over IPC. It can change in any way between releases. Incompatible changes renumber `makeUnstableChain`, so old clients get an error instead of calling the wrong methods.

Methods can move from `UnstableChain` to `Chain` once we're willing to support them for external use. `test/functional/interface_ipc.py` shows a Python client calling both interfaces. Like the existing IPC interfaces, these are only available to processes that can connect to the IPC socket, which already grants full node access through `Init.makeRpc`.

**Merge order:** This depends on bitcoin-core/libmultiprocess#377 and a subtree update that includes it (this PR currently carries that subtree change as its first commit), and on #36520, which fixes node crashes IPC clients could trigger with invalid `Chain` arguments.

---

This PR is part of the [process separation project](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/28722).

**This is based on a `src/ipc/libmultiprocess` subtree update to d1aff664fa2.** The non-base commits are:

pulls.title: net: option to disallow v1 connection on ipv4 and ipv6 peers
pulls.body:
resolves #29618.

This PR adds a config flag option `-v2onlyclearnet` which disallows outbound v1 connections on ipv4 and ipv6 networks since they're unencrypted. outbound v1 connections are still possible from tor/i2p/cjdns peers since they're encrypted networks.

- v1 outbound connections to peers are not attempted
- v1 reconnections are not attempted (if peer is falsely advertised as v2 peer and we attempt a v2 connection but it fails, we do not attempt a v1 reconnection when `-v2onlyclearnet` is switched on)

Currently 70% of reachable nodes in network supporting v2 (according to https://21.ninja/reachable-nodes/node-service-share/ and https://bitnodes.io/nodes). Also found 81% of addresses supporting v2 in the addrman of nodes I checked - personal node and the nodes in [peer.observer](https://peer.observer/addrman/alice). (You can use [this branch ](https://github.com/stratospher/bitcoin/commits/addrinfo_service_display/)to check the % of v2 addresses in a node's addrman.)

EDIT: see [summary](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/30951#issuecomment-4346061700) on pros and cons for whether to allow v2 inbounds or not for `-v2onlyclearnet`.

pulls.title: wallet: harden the read-only BDB parser against crafted files
pulls.body:
The read-only BDB parser in migrate.cpp runs on any file passed to `migratewallet`
(RPC or GUI) or `bitcoin-wallet`. #34959 added checks for btree levels and overflow
lengths, which stop simple cycles, but a crafted file can still make the parser hang
or use a lot of memory:

- A btree page can be the child of more than one internal page. Its level still
  checks out, so it gets parsed again for every path that reaches it. On master an
  ~8 KB file built this way doesn't finish.
- An overflow page with no data doesn't count toward the length #34959 checks, so
  two such pages pointing at each other loop forever. Separately, any number of
  records can point at the same overflow chain, and each one reads and stores its
  own copy.
- All of a page's index entries can point at the same record, which then gets read
  and kept once per entry. A single 64 KB page can turn into ~500 MB this way. On
  master a 256 KB file took `migratewallet` from 54 MB to ~800 MB.

The first two are fixed by tracking visited pages (the approach from #34946): btree
pages in one set, and overflow pages in another that covers the whole tree. For the
third, a page is rejected once its records add up to more than the page size.

This shouldn't affect real wallets. In a valid btree every page has a single parent
and every overflow page belongs to a single record. Records on a page can't overlap
either, since the parser already rejects databases that allow duplicates.

Each fix comes with a test in db_tests.cpp that builds the bad file by hand, plus a
test that a page filled to the last byte still parses. `wallet_migration.py` passes
with v28.2.

The last commit adds two errors from #34959 to the `wallet_bdb_parser` fuzz target.
They were missing, so the target aborted on inputs that reach them. I ran into this
while feeding mutated copies of the test files through the target.

Supersedes #35992.

pulls.title: descriptor: Reconstruct a multipath descriptor from its expansion
pulls.body:
#36442 allows multipath descriptors to be represented in a single `Descriptor` object. `GetMultipathExpansion` returns the multiple descriptors represented by a multipath descriptor. This expansion is reversible - given the expansion in the order of the multipath elements, it is possible to determine what the original multipath descriptor was. This PR adds `ReconstructMultipath` to produce a new `Descriptor` representing the multipath descriptor that produced the expansion.

Depends on #36442

pulls.title: wallet: Store information about created and imported multipath descriptors
pulls.body:
The wallet does not store any information about multipath descriptors. When a multipath descriptor is imported, it is first expanded, then the expansion descriptors are imported into the wallet.

This PR adds a field to `WalletDescriptor` which stores the IDs of the ScriptPubKeyMans of the descriptors that are part of the expansion, in the order that they are expanded. This allows us to use `ReconstructMultipath` to produce the multipath descriptor when necessary.

This is useful for working with hardware wallets that require policy registration, particularly those that require resending the descriptor that was registered.

`listdescriptors` is updated to include a `multipath_descriptor` field which contains the multipath descriptor for each individual descriptor if it originally came from a multipath descriptor.

Lastly, the automatically generated descriptors are now produced and stored as multipath descriptors, so `listdescriptors` will provide a `multipath_descriptor` for everything that the wallet automatically generates.

Note that the IDs stored in the wallet are ScriptPubKeyMan IDs, which we cannot compute from a descriptor as we assume to be opaque blobs since #35445.

Alternative to #36133, depends on #36442 and #36443

pulls.title: [RFC] Scheduled transaction broadcast, minimal
pulls.body:
Minimal implementation for "Scheduled Transaction Broadcast" new feature.

Goal: Allow a user to submit a transaction to be broadcast later, at a specified time (block height). This can be done for convenience, or to hide the exact time of the transaction creation (for increased privacy).

Goal in this PR: Extend the `sendrawtransaction` RPC with an option to schedule the broadcast at a later time, determined by the lock time of the transaction.

Use case details, with the limitations of the current changeset:
- `sendrawtransaction` has an optional parameter, `delay_after_lock_time`
- If `delay_after_lock_time` is set to 0, the `nLockTime` of the transaction determines the scheduled broadcast time (in the future).
- If `delay_after_lock_time` is set to a positive number, the broadcast time will be the sum of the transaction `nLockTime` and the parameter value.
- Only height-based lock times are supported, time-based can be added later.
- Scheduled broadcast is only supported with private broadcast.
- What is a typical delay time? 3-12 blocks. (Too long times can get problematic: risk fee increase, node restart.)
- Pending transactions are NOT persisted, so pending transactions will be lost during a node stop/restart/crash (can be added later).
- Validation should happen at both submission time and broadcast time, but now this is not true, see below.
- If the goal is to conceal the real transaction creation time, the user should add a relatively short, random period to the current time (e.g between 3-12 blocks).
- No special handling for sudden fee increase situations.
- Pending (submitted but not yet broadcast) transactions can be inspected via existing `getprivatebroadcastinfo` RPC.
- The (pre-existing) `abortprivatebroadcast` RPC can be used to cancel a pending transaction submission.
- No special support from the wallet subsystem. (A submitted but not broadcast transactions is not visible in the wallet.)
- It is possible intentionally set the locktime of a TX in the past (e.g. as a measure against wallet fingerprinting), and still use a later schedule time -- `delay_after_lock_time` with a positive value can be used to distance the submission time from the lock time.

Solution Details:
- The solution is based on the Private Broadcast implementation. 
- Transactions are stored in the already-existing `m_transactions` collection.
- A scheduled periodic check is added to check for transactions that have became due. The implementation is very similar to the existing retry logic (`ReattemptPrivateBroadcast`). Alternative: triggered by new blocks.
- Queue is not persisted currently, to be added later.
- Submit-time validation is skipped, as it would fail, due to the future locktime. To be added later.

Further improvements:
- Add a cap on the time lock, on how far in the future it is acceptable, e.g. max 7 days / 1008 blocks.
- Support time-based locktime as well. Interpret `delay_after_lock_time` in _10-minute_ units if time-based lock is used.
- At submission time, perform validation but without timelock checks. This requires a small validation change (add bypass timelocks options to methods `ProcessTransaction` and `AcceptToMemoryPool`).
- Persist the queue with pending broadcasts, so scheduled broadcasts survive node restarts.

Related issue: #34118

EDIT (Nov-03): Reworked, see https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/36429#issuecomment-6315408546

pulls.title: wallet, sqlite: Enable secure_delete by default
pulls.body:
Currently, when we make deletions or updates to the database that require records to be fully deleted and to not persist in free pages afterwards, we need to explicitly call `WalletDatabase::Rewrite`. This behavior was introduced in #635 to ensure that unencrypted private keys are erased from the database after encrypting a wallet, and initial encryption is the only consumer of this function.

However, initial encryption is not the only functionality that requires secure deletion. l0rinc's LLMs recently found changing the passphrase can leave the original that encryption key record in free pages. We should want to ensure that those records are also deleted, although I do not consider that the presence of such records in free space to actually be a problem. Note that this behavior appears to be present since wallet encryption was initially introduced in #352.

Fortunately, SQLite offers a secure_delete flag that can be enabled on each connection to a database. If set, all deletes or updates will ensure that any data that was deleted or overwritten actually are overwritten with 0's. It is one of the 2 methods in SQLite's documentation for ensuring that records do not persist in free pages, the other method being to call `VACUUM` after deletions or updates, which is what `Rewrite` does.

The downside is that secure_delete will increase CPU and disk I/O, which is why this was not set previously. However, it seems like several distros ship with secure_delete enabled by default: [Debian](https://sources.debian.org/src/sqlite3/3.54.1-2/debian/rules#L48#:~:text=DSQLITE_SECURE_DELETE), [Ubuntu](https://git.launchpad.net/ubuntu/+source/sqlite3/plain/debian/rules#:~:text=DSQLITE_SECURE_DELETE), [Fedora](https://src.fedoraproject.org/rpms/sqlite/raw/rawhide/f/sqlite.spec#:~:text=DSQLITE_SECURE_DELETE=1), [Arch](https://gitlab.archlinux.org/archlinux/packaging/packages/sqlite/-/raw/main/PKGBUILD#:~:text=DSQLITE_SECURE_DELETE), and [NixOS](https://github.com/NixOS/nixpkgs/blob/nixos-26.05/pkgs/development/libraries/sqlite/default.nix#L184) all set SQLite's compile time option to default secure_delete to enabled, and these are just the ones I've looked at. This suggests to me that the performance penalty is not actually that bad. As I run Arch and often do not use depends builds, I had not noticed that secure_delete was always on and did not experience any particularly poor wallet performance that could be attributed to that behavior. In the grand scheme of things, erases and updates are fairly infrequent in the wallet.

This PR enables secure_delete when the database is opened, and also enables it by default in the sqlite depends package. There are also a couple tests to check that all records we want deleted actually are being deleted from the database. `WalletDatabase::Rewrite` is removed as it it is no longer used.

pulls.title: wallet: fix migration with watch-only transactions
pulls.body:
Fixes #36483

As described in the linked issue, migration to descriptor wallets currently fails for legacy wallets that contain no spendable keys and are tracking watch-only transactions.

When a database transaction containing `RemoveTxs()` is aborted, the database rolls back and the registered `on_abort` callback is invoked. The current listener contains an empty `std::function` so calling it throws `std::bad_function_call` and masks the actual migration error.

The first commit changes the callback to a no-op function since no memory cleanup happens on abort. It also adds a unit test to confirm that abort restores the database record and leaves wallet memory unchanged.

After this commit, the [functional test](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/36483) supplied by the issue's author changes from `bad_function_call` to `Error: Not all transaction records were migrated (-4)`, exposing the migration error previously masked by the abort callback exception.

During wallet migration, `RemoveTxs()` defers deletion of transactions from the original wallet's in-memory `mapWallet` until after the database commit. The current check that requires an empty map before the database commit causes migration to fail.

The second commit moves the check for an empty `mapWallet` to after `RunWithinTxn()` commits the database transaction and runs the commit callback, when transactions marked for removal have been deleted.

A new functional test is added to cover migration of a blank wallet with watch-only transactions. It checks that the destination watch-only wallet retains both transactions and balance, including after unloading and reloading the wallet, without rescanning the blockchain.

pulls.title: wallet: Clear streams before advancing BDB cursor
pulls.body:
This fixes a case where migratewallet can reject an old wallet as corrupt, i.e. this occurs on wallets used in Bitcoin Knots. The v2 key metadata may include an extra flag byte that Core’s metadata loader leaves unread. 

LoadRecords reuses its key and value streams between records. BerkeleyROCursor::Next() appends to those streams, so unread bytes from one record become part of the next and can cause a deserialization error.

Clear both streams before copying the next record, matching SQLiteCursor::Next(). This keeps the existing metadata parsing and migration code.

The regression test reads two records while leaving part of the first key and value unread, then checks that the second record replaces both outputs.

Testing on Linux:
- Without the fix, the regression fails both stream-content checks.
- With the fix, test_bitcoin --run_test=db_tests passes all tests

pulls.title: net: stop using a socket once a wait reports an error
pulls.body:
ConnMan and the HTTP server would still try to read (and send) when a wait reports ErrorEvent. This means they could still read even when a read was not requested.

On select() based platform (BSDs, macOS and Windows), ErrorEvent can be returned if a peer sends us urgent data (we register the exception set because of a Windows quirk). However we can't read that urgent data, and this means we could be continuously woken up.

There is a number of things we could do to improve the situation here (see discussions in #36761), but in the meantime fix this bug by simply disconnecting immediately upon error. For consistency, adopt the same behaviour across all callers.

This PR is an alternative to #36716.

pulls.title: validation: Ensure Invalid ValidationState has result
pulls.body:
Block and transaction validation results are represented in `ValidationState`, and invalid results in "Invalid" states. Invalid validation results have a `result`, an enum value, and a `reject_reason`, a structured string.

The change is to ensure that an __invalid result always has a set result and reject reason__. This increases code robustness/security.

One instance was identified where the result was not set, and is being fixed by a new `BLOCK_INCONCLUSIVE` result. PR #31981 moved a previous-block check from outside of `TestBlockValidity()` to inside it, and introduced a new usage of `BlockValidationState` with unset result. The result field is not checked outside. This instance is changed now to use the newly-introduced `BLOCK_INCONCLUSIVE` value.

The new enum value is added to the kernel C API and its C++ wrapper. In P2P, a `BLOCK_INCONCLUSIVE` result does not lead to punishing the peer.

A few test-only instances with empty reject reason are changed to use a dummy value ("dummy-reason").

History: this was found on the side of #35570, but left untouched there; see https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/35570#issuecomment-5739477357 and https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/35570#discussion_r4075379069.

Alternatives considered:

1. Use a new reject reason enum. This is the cleanest solution, but the cost is the extension of a widely-used validation enum.
2. Use a different mechanism for returning this specific case from `TestBlockValidity()`, e.g. using `util::Expected`, as you discussed. No need to touch the `BlockValidationResult` enum. However, in the call sites of `TestBlockValidity()`, the reject reason and debug strings are handled similarly to other non-valid check results, and they would need a special handling.
3. Reuse an exisiting reject reason enum value in `TestBlockValidity()`, with the comment "only in this spot it means a little different thing".
4. Create a special `TestBlockValidationResult`, "on top of" `BlockValidationResult`, with the extra value, and a special `TestBlockValidationState` (`ValidationState<TestBlockValidationResult>`). Use this in `TestBlockValidity()`. As this is used only internally, within this methods and at its call sites, the new value+state doesn't have to be exposed. Therefore the change has lower impact.

pulls.title: ci: Share qa-assets across GitHub Actions jobs
pulls.body:
CI jobs download the same qa-assets inputs separately. As reported in #36814, these repeated requests can fail with HTTP 504 before the tests start.

Add one preparation job that checks out qa-assets once per workflow run and shares the unit-test data and fuzz corpus through Actions artifacts. Linux, macOS and Windows consumers verify the selected revision and file hashes before using them.

Containers mount the shared inputs read-only. Fuzz jobs use separate writable copies. Standalone CI scripts keep direct acquisition through the common download helper.
